resources.title: California quail
resources.description: Identify California quail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: California quail (Callipepla californica) can be identified as follows: Plump gray-and-brown quail with a forward-drooping black head plume; males have a black face bordered in white. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

keyFacts.value: Pacific western North America with introductions

identification.text: Plump gray-and-brown quail with a forward-drooping black head plume; males have a black face bordered in white.

habitat.text: Brushy foothills, farm edges and suburbs of the Pacific states, with introduced populations in British Columbia and elsewhere.

resources.quickAnswer: Chukar (Alectoris chukar) can be identified as follows: Gray-brown partridge with a red bill and legs, a black band from the eye around the throat, and boldly barred flanks. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

habitat.text: Introduced; steep, rocky arid slopes and canyons of the western United States and southern British Columbia.

resources.quickAnswer: Dusky grouse (Dendragapus obscurus) can be identified as follows: Large dark grouse; males are slate-gray with a black tail and, in display, a red neck patch bordered by white feathers. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Gambel's quail (Callipepla gambelii) can be identified as follows: Gray quail with a forward-drooping head plume and chestnut flanks; males have a black belly patch and a rusty crown. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.description: Identify Greater prairie-chicken, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Greater prairie-chicken (Tympanuchus cupido) can be identified as follows: Barred brown grouse with a short dark tail; displaying males inflate orange neck sacs and raise long neck feathers. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.title: Greater sage-grouse
resources.description: Identify Greater sage-grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus) can be identified as follows: The largest North American grouse: mottled gray-brown with a black belly and a long pointed tail; displaying males show white chest ruffs and yellow air sacs. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

habitat.text: Sagebrush steppe of the western United States and very limited parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan.

resources.title: Gunnison sage-grouse
resources.description: Identify Gunnison sage-grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Gunnison sage-grouse is a smaller relative of greater sage-grouse found only in southwestern Colorado and southeastern Utah. Do not shoot unless you are certain of the species.

identification.text: Smaller than greater sage-grouse, with bold white bands across the tail and thicker plumes behind the head in displaying males.
Tail: Gunnison sage-grouse show distinct pale bands across the tail; greater sage-grouse tails are more uniformly marked.
Size: Gunnison sage-grouse are about one-third smaller than greater sage-grouse.
Range: the two species do not overlap; any sage-grouse in southwestern Colorado or southeastern Utah should be treated as Gunnison until the responsible authority's map says otherwise.

habitat.text: Sagebrush of southwestern Colorado and southeastern Utah only.

resources.title: Sooty grouse
resources.description: Identify Sooty grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Sooty grouse (Dendragapus fuliginosus) can be identified as follows: Large dark grouse very like dusky grouse; displaying males show a yellow neck patch, and the tail usually has a gray band. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: White-tailed ptarmigan (Lagopus leucura) can be identified as follows: The smallest ptarmigan: an all-white tail in every season, white in winter and mottled gray-brown in summer. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: The smallest ptarmigan: an all-white tail in every season, white in winter and mottled gray-brown in summer.
